SHALLOW. That we have, that we have, that we have; in faith, Sir John, we have. Our watchword was "Hem boys!" Come, let's go to dinner; come, let's go to dinner. Jesus, the days that we have seen! Come, come.
[Exeunt Falstaff, Shallow and Silence.]

BULLCALF. Good Master Corporate Bardolph, stand my friend; and here's four Harry ten shillings in French crowns for you. In very truth, sir, I would as soon be hanged, sir, as go. And yet, for my own part, sir, I do not care; but rather because I am unwilling, and, for my own part, have a desire to stay with my friends; otherwise, sir, I would not care, for my own part, so much.
BARDOLPH. Get on, stand aside.

MOULDY. And, good Master Corporal Captain, for my old dame's sake, stand my friend. She has nobody to do anything around her when I am gone, and she is old, and cannot help herself. You shall have forty, sir.
BARDOLPH. Get on, stand aside.

FEEBLE. By my faith, I don't care. A man can die only once. We owe God a death. I'll never bear a base mind. If it be my destiny, so be it; if it be not, so. No man's too good to serve his prince, and let it go which way it will, he who dies this year is quit for the next.
BARDOLPH. Well said, you're a good fellow.
FEEBLE. Faith, I'll bear no base mind.
[Enter Falstaff and the Justices.]
FALSTAFF. Come, sir, which men shall I have?
SHALLOW. Four of whichever you please.
BARDOLPH. Sir, a word with you. I have three pounds to free Mouldy and Bullcalf.
FALSTAFF. Get on, well.
SHALLOW. Come, Sir John, which four will you have?
FALSTAFF. You choose for me.
SHALLOW. By Mary, then, Mouldy, Bullcalf, Feeble, and Shadow.
FALSTAFF. Mouldy and Bullcalf: as for you, Mouldy, stay at home till you are past service; and for your part, Bullcalf, grow till you come up to it. I'll have none of you.
SHALLOW. Sir John, Sir John, do not yourself wrong. They are your likeliest men, and I would have you served with the best.

FALSTAFF. Will you tell me, Master Shallow, how to choose a man? Do I care for the limb, the sinews, the stature, bulk, and big assemblage of a man? Give me the spirit, Master Shallow. Here's Wart. You see what a ragged appearance it is. He shall load and fire at you with the motion of a pewterer's hammer, come off and on swifter than he that ties up the hangman's bucket. And this same half-faced fellow, Shadow; give me this man. He presents no mark to the enemy. The enemy might as well aim at the edge of a penknife. And for a retreat, how swiftly will this Feeble, the woman's tailor, run off! Oh, give me the spare men, and spare me the great ones. Put a caliver into Wart's hand, Bardolph.
BARDOLPH. Hold, Wart. Traverse. Thus, thus, thus.

FALSTAFF. Come, manage me your caliver. So, very well, get on, very good, exceedingly good. Oh, give me always a little, lean, old, chapped, bald shot. Well said, in faith, Wart. You're a good scab. Hold, here's a tester for you.

SHALLOW. He is not his craft's master, he doesn't do it right. I remember at Mile-End Green, when I lay at Clement's Inn — I was then Sir Dagonet in Arthur's show — there was a little quivering fellow, and he would manage you his weapon thus. And he would about and about, and come in and come in. "Rah, tah, tah," he would say. "Bounce" he would say; and away again he would go, and again he would come. I shall never see such a fellow.

FALSTAFF. These fellows will do well. Master Shallow. God keep you, Master Silence: I will not use many words with you. Fare you well, gentlemen both. I thank you. I must do a dozen miles tonight. Bardolph, give the soldiers coats.
SHALLOW. Sir John, the Lord bless you! God prosper your affairs! God send us peace! At your return, visit our house, let our old acquaintance be renewed. Perhaps I will go with you to the court.
FALSTAFF. Before God, I wish you would, Master Shallow.
SHALLOW. Get on, I have spoken in a word. God keep you.

FALSTAFF. Fare you well, gentle gentlemen. [Exeunt Justices.] On, Bardolph, lead the men away. [Exeunt Bardolph, recruits, etc.] As I return, I will fetch off these justices. I see the bottom of Justice Shallow. Lord, Lord, how subject we old men are to this vice of lying! This same starved justice has done nothing but prate to me of the wildness of his youth, and the feats he has done about Turnbull Street, and every third word a lie, more punctually paid to the hearer than the Turk's tribute. I do remember him at Clement's Inn, like a man made after supper from a cheese-paring. When he was naked, he was, for all the world, like a forked radish, with a head fantastically carved upon it with a knife. He was so forlorn, that his dimensions to any thick sight were invisible. He was the very genius of famine, yet lecherous as a monkey, and the whores called him mandrake. He came ever in the rearward of the fashion, and sang to the worn-out hussies those tunes he heard the carmen whistle, and swore they were his own fancies or his good-nights. And now this Vice's dagger has become a squire, and talks as familiarly of John of Gaunt as if he had been sworn brother to him, and I'll be sworn he never saw him but once in the tilt-yard, and then he burst his head for crowding among the marshal's men. I saw it and told John of Gaunt he beat his own name, for you might have thrust him and all his clothing into an eel-skin; the case of a treble oboe was a mansion for him, a court. And now he has land and beef-cattle. Well, I'll be acquainted with him if I return, and it shall go hard but I'll make him a philosopher's two stones to me. If the young dace is bait for the old pike, I see no reason in the law of nature why I may not snap at him. Let time shape, and there an end.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — Yorkshire. Gaultree Forest
paragraphs: [Enter the Archbishop of York, Mowbray, Hastings and others.]
ARCHBISHOP. What is this forest called?
HASTINGS. It is Gaultree Forest, if it please your Grace.
ARCHBISHOP. Halt here, my lords, and send out scouts to learn the numbers of our enemies.
HASTINGS. We have already sent them out.

ARCHBISHOP. That is well done. My friends and brothers in these great affairs, I must let you know that I have received recently dated letters from Northumberland, their cold intent, tone, and substance thus: He wishes here his person, with such forces as might match his rank, which he could not muster; whereupon he has retired, to ripen his growing fortunes, to Scotland, and concludes with hearty prayers that your attempts may outlive the hazard and fearful meeting with their opponents.
MOWBRAY. Thus the hopes we have in him touch ground and dash themselves to pieces.
[Enter a Messenger.]
HASTINGS. Now, what news?
MESSENGER. West of this forest, scarcely off a mile, the enemy comes on in fine formation, and, by the ground they cover, I judge their number to be upon or near the count of thirty thousand.
MOWBRAY. The exact proportion we reckoned them at. Let's move on and face them in the field.
[Enter Westmoreland.]
ARCHBISHOP. What well-equipped leader confronts us here?
MOWBRAY. I think it is my Lord of Westmoreland.
WESTMORELAND. Health and fair greeting from our general, the prince, Lord John and Duke of Lancaster.
ARCHBISHOP. Speak on, my Lord of Westmoreland, in peace, what concerns your coming.

WESTMORELAND. Then, my lord, to your Grace I chiefly address the substance of my speech. If rebellion came in its own form, in base and abject crowds, led on by bloody youth, guarded with rags, and supported by boys and beggary; I say, if damned uprising appeared in its true, native, and most proper shape, you, reverend father, and these noble lords would not be here to dress the ugly form of base and bloody insurrection with your fair honors. You, Lord Archbishop, whose see is maintained by civil peace, whose beard the silver hand of peace has touched, whose learning and good letters peace has tutored, whose white robes signify innocence, the dove and very blessed spirit of peace, why do you so badly translate yourself out of the speech of peace, which bears such grace, into the harsh and boisterous tongue of war; turning your books to graves, your ink to blood, your pens to lances, and your divine tongue to a loud trumpet and a call to war?

ARCHBISHOP. Why do I this? So the question stands. Briefly to this end: we are all diseased, and with our overindulgence and reckless hours have brought ourselves into a burning fever, and we must bleed for it; of which disease our late King Richard, being infected, died. But, my most noble Lord of Westmoreland, I do not take on myself here as a physician, nor do I as an enemy to peace troop in the throngs of military men, but rather appear awhile like fearful war to discipline rank minds sick of happiness, and purge the obstructions which begin to stop our very veins of life. Hear me more plainly. I have justly weighed in equal balance what wrongs our arms may do, what wrongs we suffer, and find our grievances heavier than our offences. We see which way the stream of time runs, and are forced from our most quiet there by the rough torrent of occasion, and have the summary of all our grievances, when time shall serve, to show in articles; which long before this we offered to the King and could by no suit gain our audience. When we are wronged and would unfold our grievances, we are denied access to his person even by those men who have most wronged us. The dangers of the days just gone, whose memory is written on the earth with still-appearing blood, and the examples of every minute's instance, present now, have put us into these unbecoming arms, not to break peace or any branch of it, but to establish here a peace indeed, agreeing both in name and quality.

WESTMORELAND. Whenever yet was your appeal denied? Wherein have you been galled by the King? What peer has been suborned to grate on you, that you should seal this lawless bloody book of forged rebellion with a divine seal and consecrate uprising's bitter edge?
ARCHBISHOP. My brother general, the commonwealth, to a brother born a household cruelty, I make my quarrel particular.
WESTMORELAND. There is no need of any such redress, or if there were, it does not belong to you.
MOWBRAY. Why not to him in part, and to us all who feel the bruises of the days before, and suffer the condition of these times to lay a heavy and unequal hand upon our honors?

WESTMORELAND. Oh, my good Lord Mowbray, interpret the times according to their necessities, and you shall say indeed, it is the time, and not the King, that does you injuries. Yet for your part, it does not appear to me either from the King or in the present time that you should have an inch of any ground to build a grievance on. Were you not restored to all the Duke of Norfolk's lordships, your noble and right well-remembered father's?

MOWBRAY. What thing, in honor, had my father lost, that needed to be revived and breathed in me? The King who loved him, as the state stood then, was forced perforce to banish him, and then that Henry Bolingbroke and he, being mounted and both roused in their seats, their neighing horses daring of the spur, their armed lances in charge, their visors down, their eyes of fire sparkling through eye-slits of steel, and the loud trumpet blowing them together, then, then, when there was nothing that could have kept my father from the breast of Bolingbroke, oh, when the King threw his warder down, his own life hung upon the staff he threw; then he threw down himself and all their lives that by indictment and by force of sword have since perished under Bolingbroke.

WESTMORELAND. You speak, Lord Mowbray, now you know not what. The Earl of Hereford was reputed then in England the most valiant gentleman. Who knows on whom fortune would then have smiled? But if your father had been victor there, he would never have borne it out of Coventry; for all the country in a general voice cried hate upon him; and all their prayers and love were set on Hereford, whom they doted on and blessed and graced, indeed more than the King. But this is mere digression from my purpose. Here I come from our princely general to know your grievances, to tell you from his Grace that he will give you audience; and wherein it shall appear that your demands are just, you shall enjoy them, everything set aside that might even think you enemies.
MOWBRAY. But he has forced us to compel this offer, and it proceeds from policy, not love.

WESTMORELAND. Mowbray, you overestimate to take it so; this offer comes from mercy, not from fear. For, lo, within view our army lies, upon my honor, all too confident to give admittance to a thought of fear. Our battle line is more full of names than yours, our men more perfect in the use of arms, our armor all as strong, our cause the best; then reason will that our hearts should be as good. Don't say then that our offer is compelled.
MOWBRAY. Well, by my will we shall admit no parley.
WESTMORELAND. That argues only the shame of your offence: a rotten case abides no handling.
HASTINGS. Has Prince John a full commission, in very ample authority from his father, to hear and absolutely to determine of what conditions we shall stand upon?
WESTMORELAND. That is implied in the general's name: I wonder you make so slight a question.

ARCHBISHOP. Then take, my Lord of Westmoreland, this schedule, for this contains our general grievances. Each separate article herein redressed, all members of our cause, both here and hence, who are bound by sinew to this action, acquitted by a true substantial form and present execution of our wills to us and to our purposes confined, we will come within our awful banks again and knit our powers to the arm of peace.

WESTMORELAND. This I will show the general. Please you, lords, in sight of both our battle lines we may meet, and either end in peace, which God so frame! Or call to the place of difference the swords which must decide it.
ARCHBISHOP. My lord, we will do so.
[Exit Westmoreland.]
MOWBRAY. There is a thing within my bosom that tells me that no conditions of our peace can stand.
HASTINGS. Fear not that: if we can make our peace upon such large terms and so absolute as our conditions shall consist of, our peace shall stand as firm as rocky mountains.

MOWBRAY. Yes, but our worth shall be such that every slight and false-derived cause, yes, every idle, fastidious, and wanton reason, shall to the King taste of this action; that, were our royal faiths martyrs in love, we shall be winnowed with so rough a wind that even our corn shall seem as light as chaff and good from bad find no partition.

ARCHBISHOP. No, no, my lord. Note this; the King is weary of dainty and such picking grievances; for he has found to end one doubt by death revives two greater in the heirs of life; and therefore he will wipe his tables clean and keep no telltale to his memory that may repeat and historicize his loss to new remembrance. For full well he knows he cannot so precisely weed this land as his mistrustings give occasion. His foes are so rooted with his friends that, plucking to unfix an enemy, he does unfasten so and shake a friend. So that this land, like an offensive wife that has enraged him on to offer blows, as he is striking, holds his infant up and hangs resolved correction in the arm that was lifted to execution.

HASTINGS. Besides, the King has worn out all his rods on recent offenders, so that he now lacks the very instruments of chastisement; so that his power, like a fangless lion, may threaten, but not hold.
ARCHBISHOP. It is very true, and therefore be assured, my good Lord Marshal, if we now make our atonement well, our peace will, like a broken limb united, grow stronger for the breaking.
MOWBRAY. Be it so. Here is returned my Lord of Westmoreland.
[Enter Westmoreland.]
WESTMORELAND. The prince is here at hand. Does it please your lordship to meet his Grace at a fair distance between our armies?
MOWBRAY. Your Grace of York, in God's name then set forward.
ARCHBISHOP. Go before, and greet his Grace. My lord, we come.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — Another part of the forest
paragraphs: [Enter, from one side, Mowbray, attended; afterwards, the Archbishop, Hastings, and others; from the other side, Prince John of Lancaster, and Westmoreland; Officers, and others with them.]

LANCASTER. You are well met here, my cousin Mowbray. Good day to you, gentle Lord Archbishop; and so to you, Lord Hastings, and to all. My Lord of York, it suited you better when your flock, assembled by the bell, encircled you to hear with reverence your exposition on the holy text, than now to see you here an iron man, cheering on a mob of rebels with your drum, turning the word to the sword, and life to death. The man that sits within a monarch's heart, and ripens in the sunshine of his favor, if he abused the countenance of the king, alas, what mischief might he set going in the shadow of such greatness! With you, Lord Bishop, it is exactly so. Who has not heard it said how deep you were in the books of God, to us the speaker in his parliament, to us the imagined voice of God himself, the very opener and go-between between the grace, the sanctities of heaven, and our dull workings? Oh, who shall believe but that you misuse the reverence of your place, employ the countenance and grace of heaven as a false favorite does his prince's name, in dishonorable deeds? You have taken up, under the counterfeit zeal of God, the subjects of his deputy, my father, and both against the peace of heaven and him have here swarmed them up.

ARCHBISHOP. Good my Lord of Lancaster, I am not here against your father's peace; but, as I told my Lord of Westmoreland, the time, disordered, does, in common sense, crowd us and crush us into this monstrous form to hold our safety up. I sent your Grace the parcels and particulars of our grievance, which has been scornfully shoved from the court, whereon this Hydra son of war is born, whose dangerous eyes may well be charmed asleep with the granting of our most just and right desires, and true obedience, of this madness cured, will stoop tamely to the foot of majesty.
MOWBRAY. If not, we are ready to try our fortunes to the last man.

HASTINGS. And though we here fall down, we have supplies to second our attempt: if they miscarry, theirs shall second them; and so a succession of mischief shall be born, and heir to heir shall hold this quarrel up while England shall have any generation.
LANCASTER. You are too shallow, Hastings, much too shallow, to sound the bottom of the times to come.
WESTMORELAND. May it please your Grace to answer them directly how far you approve their articles.

LANCASTER. I like them all, and approve them well, and swear here, by the honor of my blood, that my father's purposes have been misunderstood, and some about him have too lavishly twisted his meaning and authority. My lord, these grievances shall be redressed with speed; upon my soul, they shall. If this may please you, discharge your forces to their several counties, as we will ours; and here between the armies let's drink together in friendship and embrace, that all their eyes may carry those tokens home of our restored love and amity.
ARCHBISHOP. I take your princely word for these redresses.
LANCASTER. I give it to you, and will maintain my word; and thereupon I drink to your Grace.
HASTINGS. Go, captain, and deliver to the army this news of peace. Let them have their pay, and part. I know it will please them. Hurry, captain.
[Exit Officer.]
ARCHBISHOP. To you, my noble Lord of Westmoreland.
WESTMORELAND. I pledge your Grace; and if you knew what pains I have taken to breed this present peace, you would drink freely; but my love to you shall show itself more openly hereafter.
ARCHBISHOP. I do not doubt you.
WESTMORELAND. I am glad of it. Health to my lord and gentle cousin, Mowbray.
MOWBRAY. You wish me health at a very happy moment, for I am suddenly something ill.
ARCHBISHOP. Against ill chances men are ever merry, but heaviness foreruns the good event.
WESTMORELAND. Therefore be merry, cousin, since sudden sorrow serves to say thus, "Some good thing comes tomorrow."
ARCHBISHOP. Believe me, I am exceedingly light in spirit.
MOWBRAY. So much the worse, if your own rule be true.
[Shouts within.]
LANCASTER. The word of peace is delivered. Hear how they shout!
MOWBRAY. This would have been cheerful after victory.
ARCHBISHOP. A peace is of the nature of a conquest; for then both parties nobly are subdued, and neither party loser.
LANCASTER. Go, my lord. And let our army be discharged too.
[Exit Westmoreland.]
And, good my lord, if it please you, let our forces march by us, that we may look over the men we should have fought with.
ARCHBISHOP. Go, good Lord Hastings, and, before they are dismissed, let them march by.
[Exit Hastings.]
LANCASTER. I trust, lords, we shall lie tonight together.
[Enter Westmoreland.]
Now, cousin, why does our army still stand?
WESTMORELAND. The leaders, having orders from you to stand, will not go off until they hear you speak.
LANCASTER. They know their duties.
[Enter Hastings.]

HASTINGS. My lord, our army is dispersed already. Like youthful steers unyoked, they take their courses east, west, north, south; or, like a school let out, each hurries toward his home and sporting place.
WESTMORELAND. Good tidings, my Lord Hastings; for which I arrest you, traitor, of high treason; and you, Lord Archbishop, and you, Lord Mowbray, of capital treason I attach you both.
MOWBRAY. Is this proceeding just and honorable?
WESTMORELAND. Is your assembly so?
ARCHBISHOP. Will you thus break your faith?

LANCASTER. I pledged you none. I promised you redress of these same grievances of which you complained; which, by my honor, I will perform with a most Christian care. But for you, rebels, look to taste the due fitting for rebellion and such acts as yours. Most shallowly did you commence these arms, foolishly brought here and foolishly sent hence. Strike up our drums, pursue the scattered stragglers: God, and not we, has safely fought today. Some guard these traitors to the block of death, treason's true bed and surrenderer of breath.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — Another part of the forest
paragraphs: [Alarum. Excursions. Enter Falstaff and Colevile, meeting.]
FALSTAFF. What's your name, sir? Of what rank are you, and of what place, please?
COLEVILE. I am a knight, sir, and my name is Colevile of the Dale.

FALSTAFF. Well, then, Colevile is your name, a knight is your rank, and your place the Dale. Colevile shall still be your name, a traitor your rank, and the dungeon your place, a place deep enough; so you shall still be Colevile of the Dale.
COLEVILE. Aren't you Sir John Falstaff?

FALSTAFF. As good a man as he, sir, whoever I am. Do you yield, sir, or shall I sweat for you? If I do sweat, they are the drops of your lovers, and they weep for your death. Therefore rouse up fear and trembling, and pay tribute to my mercy.
COLEVILE. I think you are Sir John Falstaff, and in that thought I yield to you.

FALSTAFF. I have a whole school of tongues in this belly of mine, and not a tongue of them all speaks any word but my name. If I had only a belly of any modest size, I would simply be the most active fellow in Europe. My womb, my womb, my womb undoes me. Here comes our general.
[Enter Prince John of Lancaster, Westmoreland, Blunt, and others.]
LANCASTER. The heat is past; pursue no further now. Call in the forces, good cousin Westmoreland.
[Exit Westmoreland.]
Now, Falstaff, where have you been all this time? When everything is ended, then you come. These tardy tricks of yours will, on my life, one time or other break some gallows' back.

FALSTAFF. I would be sorry, my lord, that it should be so. I never knew yet but that rebuke and check was the reward of valor. Do you think me a swallow, an arrow, or a bullet? Have I, in my poor and old movement, the speed of thought? I have rushed here with the very utmost inch of possibility; I have foundered nine score and odd post-horses; and here, travel-stained as I am, have in my pure and immaculate valor, taken Sir John Colevile of the Dale, a most furious knight and valorous enemy. But what of that? He saw me, and yielded; so that I may justly say, with the hook-nosed fellow of Rome, "I came, saw, and overcame."
LANCASTER. It was more of his courtesy than your deserving.

FALSTAFF. I don't know. Here he is, and here I yield him. And I beseech your Grace, let it be booked with the rest of this day's deeds, or, by the Lord, I will have it in a separate ballad otherwise, with my own picture on the top of it, Colevile kissing my foot: to which course if I be forced, if you don't all look like gilt twopences to me, and I in the clear sky of fame outshine you as much as the full moon does the cinders of the firmament, which look like pins' heads to her, then believe not the word of the noble. Therefore let me have right, and let merit mount.
LANCASTER. Yours is too heavy to mount.
FALSTAFF. Let it shine, then.
LANCASTER. Yours is too thick to shine.
FALSTAFF. Let it do something, my good lord, that may do me good, and call it what you will.
LANCASTER. Is your name Colevile?
COLEVILE. It is, my lord.
LANCASTER. A famous rebel you are, Colevile.
FALSTAFF. And a famous true subject took him.
COLEVILE. I am, my lord, just as my betters are who led me here. Had they been ruled by me, you should have won them at a dearer price than you have.
FALSTAFF. I don't know how they sold themselves, but you, like a kind fellow, gave yourself away free, and I thank you for yourself.
[Enter Westmoreland.]
LANCASTER. Now, have you left off pursuit?
WESTMORELAND. The retreat is made and execution stayed.
LANCASTER. Send Colevile with his confederates to York, for immediate execution. Blunt, lead him hence, and see you guard him securely.
[Exeunt Blunt and others with Colevile.]

And now let us hasten toward the court, my lords. I hear the King my father is gravely sick. Our news shall go before us to his Majesty, which, cousin, you shall bear to comfort him, and we with sober speed will follow you.
FALSTAFF. My lord, I beseech you give me leave to go through Gloucestershire, and, when you come to court, please stand as my good lord, in your good report.
LANCASTER. Fare you well, Falstaff. I, in my position, shall speak better of you than you deserve.
[Exeunt all but Falstaff.]

FALSTAFF. I wish you had only the wit, it would be better than your dukedom. Good faith, this same young sober-blooded boy doesn't love me, nor can a man make him laugh; but that's no marvel, he drinks no wine. There's never any of these demure boys who come to any proof; for thin drink so over-cools their blood, and making many fish meals, that they fall into a kind of male green-sickness; and then, when they marry, they beget girls. They are generally fools and cowards, which some of us would be too, but for inflammation. A good sherris-sack has a two-fold operation in it. It ascends into the brain, dries up there all the foolish and dull and curdy vapors that surround it, makes it perceptive, quick, inventive, full of nimble, fiery, and delightful shapes, which, delivered over to the voice, the tongue, which is the birth, becomes excellent wit. The second property of your excellent sherris is the warming of the blood, which, before cold and settled, left the liver white and pale, which is the badge of cowardice and pusillanimity. But the sherris warms it and makes it course from the inwards to the parts' extremes. It illuminates the face, which as a beacon gives warning to all the rest of this little kingdom, man, to arm; and then the vital commoners and inland petty spirits muster all to their captain, the heart, who, great and puffed up with this retinue, does any deed of courage; and this valor comes from sherris. So that skill with the weapon is nothing without sack, for that sets it to work; and learning is a mere hoard of gold kept by a devil, till sack commences it and sets it into act and use. Hereof it comes that Prince Harry is valiant; for the cold blood he did naturally inherit from his father he has, like lean, sterile and bare land, manured, husbanded and tilled with excellent industry of drinking good and good store of fertile sherris, so that he is become very hot and valiant. If I had a thousand sons, the first human principle I would teach them should be to forswear thin drinks and to addict themselves to sack.
[Enter Bardolph.]
How now, Bardolph?
BARDOLPH. The army is discharged all and gone.

FALSTAFF. Let them go. I'll through Gloucestershire, and there will I visit Master Robert Shallow, Esquire. I have him already softening between my finger and my thumb, and shortly will I seal with him. Come away.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 4 — Westminster. The Jerusalem Chamber
paragraphs: [Enter the King, Warwick, Thomas Duke of Clarence and Humphrey Duke of Gloucester and others.]

HENRY IV. Now, lords, if God gives a successful end to this dispute that bleeds at our doors, we will lead our youth on to higher fields and draw no swords but those that are sanctified. Our navy is ready, our forces collected, our deputies for our absence well installed, and everything lies level with our wish. Only we need a little personal strength; and we must pause until these rebels now afoot come underneath the yoke of government.
WARWICK. Both of which we don't doubt your Majesty shall soon enjoy.
HENRY IV. Humphrey, my son of Gloucester, where is the Prince your brother?
GLOUCESTER. I think he's gone to hunt, my lord, at Windsor.
HENRY IV. And how accompanied?
GLOUCESTER. I do not know, my lord.
HENRY IV. Isn't his brother Thomas of Clarence with him?
GLOUCESTER. No, my good lord, he is present here.
CLARENCE. What would my lord and father?

HENRY IV. Nothing but well to you, Thomas of Clarence. How does it happen you are not with the Prince your brother? He loves you, and you neglect him, Thomas. You have a better place in his affection than all your brothers. Cherish it, my boy, and noble offices of mediation you may perform, after I am dead, between his greatness and your other brothers. Therefore don't neglect him, don't blunt his love, nor lose the good advantage of his grace by seeming cold or careless of his will; for he is gracious, if he is treated with attention, he has a tear for pity, and a hand open as day for melting charity: yet nevertheless, being incensed, he's flint, as changeable as winter, and as sudden as squalls congealed in the morning's first light. His temper therefore must be well observed. Chide him for faults, and do it reverently, when you perceive his blood inclined to mirth; but, being moody, give him time and space, until his passions, like a whale on dry ground, exhaust themselves with thrashing. Learn this, Thomas, and you shall prove a shelter to your friends, a hoop of gold to bind your brothers in, that the united vessel of their blood, mingled with the venom of suggestion — as, perforce, the age will pour it in — shall never leak, though it work as strongly as aconite or sudden gunpowder.
CLARENCE. I shall observe him with all care and love.
HENRY IV. Why are you not at Windsor with him, Thomas?
CLARENCE. He is not there today; he dines in London.
HENRY IV. And how accompanied? Can you tell me that?
CLARENCE. With Poins, and other of his constant followers.

HENRY IV. Most subject is the richest soil to weeds, and he, the noble image of my youth, is overspread with them; therefore my grief stretches itself beyond the hour of death. Blood weeps from my heart when I shape in imaginary forms the unguided days and rotten times that you shall look upon when I am sleeping with my ancestors. For when his headstrong riot has no curb, when rage and hot blood are his counsellors, when means and lavish manners meet together, oh, with what wings shall his desires fly toward oncoming peril and opposed decay!

WARWICK. My gracious lord, you look beyond him quite. The prince only studies his companions like a strange tongue, in which, to gain the language, it's necessary that the most immodest word be looked upon and learned; which once attained, your Highness knows, comes to no further use but to be known and hated. So, like gross terms, the Prince will, in the perfection of time, cast off his followers, and their memory shall live as a pattern or a measure, by which his Grace must measure the lives of others, turning past evils to advantages.
HENRY IV. It is seldom that the bee leaves her comb in the dead carrion.
[Enter Westmoreland.]
Who's here? Westmoreland?

WESTMORELAND. Health to my sovereign, and new happiness added to what I am to deliver! Prince John your son kisses your Grace's hand. Mowbray, the Bishop Scroop, Hastings and all are brought to the correction of your law. There is not now a rebel's sword unsheathed, but Peace puts forth her olive everywhere. The manner of how this action has been carried out here at more leisure may your Highness read, with every course in its detail.
HENRY IV. Oh Westmoreland, you are a summer bird, who ever in the rear of winter sings the lifting up of day.
[Enter Harcourt.]
Look, here's more news.

HARCOURT. From enemies may heaven keep your Majesty; and when they stand against you, may they fall as those that I have come to tell you of! The Earl Northumberland and the Lord Bardolph, with a great force of English and of Scots, are overthrown by the sheriff of Yorkshire. The manner and true order of the fight this packet, if it please you, contains in full.

HENRY IV. And why should these good news make me sick? Will Fortune never come with both hands full, but write her fair words still in the foulest letters? She either gives a stomach and no food — such are the poor, in health; or else a feast and takes away the stomach — such are the rich, that have abundance and don't enjoy it. I should rejoice now at this happy news, and now my sight fails, and my brain is giddy. Oh me! Come near me, now I am very ill.
GLOUCESTER. Comfort, your Majesty!
CLARENCE. Oh my royal father!
WESTMORELAND. My sovereign lord, cheer up yourself, look up.
WARWICK. Be patient, princes; you know these fits are with his Highness very ordinary. Stand back from him, give him air; he will be well at once.
CLARENCE. No, no, he cannot long hold out these pangs. The incessant care and labor of his mind has worn the wall that should confine it in so thin that life looks through it and will break out.

GLOUCESTER. The people frighten me, for they observe fatherless heirs and loathsome births of nature. The seasons change their manners, as if the year had found some months asleep and leapt over them.
CLARENCE. The river has thrice flowed, no ebb between, and the old folk, time's doting chronicles, say it did so a little time before that our great-grandsire, Edward, sickened and died.
WARWICK. Speak lower, princes, for the King recovers.
GLOUCESTER. This apoplexy will certainly be his end.
HENRY IV. Please take me up, and bear me hence into some other chamber: softly, I beg.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 5 — Another chamber
paragraphs: [The King lying on a bed. Clarence, Gloucester, Warwick and others in attendance.]
HENRY IV. Let no noise be made, my gentle friends, unless some dull and favorable hand will whisper music to my weary spirit.
WARWICK. Call for the music in the other room.
HENRY IV. Set the crown upon my pillow here.
CLARENCE. His eye is hollow, and he is much changed.
WARWICK. Less noise, less noise!
[Enter Prince Henry.]
PRINCE HENRY. Who has seen the Duke of Clarence?
CLARENCE. I am here, brother, full of heaviness.
PRINCE HENRY. How now, rain indoors, and none outside? How is the King?
GLOUCESTER. Exceedingly ill.
PRINCE HENRY. Has he heard the good news yet? Tell it to him.
GLOUCESTER. He altered much upon hearing it.
PRINCE HENRY. If he is sick with joy, he'll recover without medicine.
WARWICK. Not so much noise, my lords. Sweet prince, speak low; the King your father is disposed to sleep.
CLARENCE. Let us withdraw into the other room.
WARWICK. Will it please your Grace to come along with us?
PRINCE HENRY. No, I will sit and watch here by the King.
[Exeunt all but the Prince.]

Why does the crown lie there upon his pillow, being so troublesome a bedfellow? Oh polished disturbance! Golden care! That keeps the gates of slumber open wide to many a watchful night! Sleep with it now; yet not so sound and half so deeply sweet as he whose brow with a homely cap bound snores out the watch of the night. Oh majesty! When you pinch your wearer, you sit like a rich armor worn in the heat of day, that scalds with safety. By his gates of breath there lies a downy feather which doesn't stir: did he breathe, that light and weightless down would of necessity move. My gracious lord, my father! This sleep is sound indeed; this is a sleep that has divorced from this golden circle so many English kings. Your due from me is tears and heavy sorrows of the blood, which nature, love, and filial tenderness, shall, oh dear father, pay you plentifully. My due from you is this imperial crown, which, as immediate from your place and blood, descends to me. See, where it sits, which God shall guard; and put the world's whole strength into one giant arm, it shall not force this hereditary honor from me. This from you I will leave to mine, as it is left to me.
[Exit.]
HENRY IV. Warwick! Gloucester! Clarence!
[Enter Warwick, Gloucester, Clarence and the rest.]
CLARENCE. Does the King call?
WARWICK. What does your Majesty want? How fares your Grace?
HENRY IV. Why did you leave me here alone, my lords?
CLARENCE. We left the Prince my brother here, my liege, who undertook to sit and watch by you.
HENRY IV. The Prince of Wales! Where is he? Let me see him. He is not here.
WARWICK. This door is open, he has gone this way.
GLOUCESTER. He did not come through the chamber where we waited.
HENRY IV. Where is the crown? Who took it from my pillow?
WARWICK. When we withdrew, my liege, we left it here.
HENRY IV. The Prince has taken it from here. Go seek him out. Is he so hasty that he supposes my sleep is my death? Find him, my Lord of Warwick, scold him hither.
[Exit Warwick.]

This part of his joins with my disease, and helps to end me. See, sons, what things you are, how quickly nature falls into revolt when gold becomes her object! For this the foolish over-careful fathers have broken their sleep with thoughts, their brains with care, their bones with industry; for this they have gathered and piled up the cankered heaps of strangely-acquired gold; for this they have been thoughtful to equip their sons with arts and martial exercises; when, like the bee, taking from every flower the virtuous sweets, our thighs packed with wax, our mouths with honey, we bring it to the hive; and like the bees, are murdered for our pains. This bitter taste yields his hoardings to the dying father.
[Enter Warwick.]
Now where is he that will not wait so long until his friend sickness has finished me?

WARWICK. My lord, I found the Prince in the next room, washing with kindly tears his gentle cheeks, with such a deep bearing in great sorrow that tyranny, which never drank but blood, would, by beholding him, have washed his knife with gentle eye-drops. He is coming here.
HENRY IV. But why did he take away the crown?
[Enter Prince Henry.]
See where he comes. Come here to me, Harry. Leave the chamber, leave us here alone.
[Exeunt Warwick and the rest.]
PRINCE HENRY. I never thought to hear you speak again.

HENRY IV. Your wish was father, Harry, to that thought. I stay too long by you, I weary you. Do you so hunger for my empty chair that you must invest yourself with my honors before your hour be ripe? Oh foolish youth! You seek the greatness that will overwhelm you. Wait just a little, for my cloud of dignity is held from falling with so weak a wind that it will quickly drop. My day is dim. You have stolen that which after some few hours would have been yours without offence, and at my death you have sealed up my expectation. Your life made it plain that you didn't love me, and you would have me die assured of it. You hid a thousand daggers in your thoughts which you have whetted on your stony heart, to stab at half an hour of my life. What, can you not bear with me half an hour? Then get you gone, and dig my grave yourself, and bid the merry bells ring in your ear that you are crowned, not that I am dead. Let all the tears that should bedew my hearse be drops of balm to sanctify your head, only compound me with forgotten dust. Give that which gave you life unto the worms. Pluck down my officers, break my decrees; for now a time is come to mock at form. Harry the Fifth is crowned. Up, vanity! Down, royal state! All you sage counsellors, away! And to the English court assemble now, from every region, apes of idleness! Now, neighboring lands, purge yourselves of your scum. Have you a ruffian that will swear, drink, dance, revel the night, rob, murder, and commit the oldest sins in the newest kinds of ways? Be happy, he will trouble you no more. England shall double-gild his treble guilt, England shall give him office, honor, might, for the fifth Harry from curbed license plucks the muzzle of restraint, and the wild dog shall sink his tooth on every innocent. Oh my poor kingdom, sick with civil blows! When my care could not hold back your riots, what will you do when riot is your care? Oh, you will be a wilderness again, peopled with wolves, your old inhabitants!

PRINCE HENRY. Oh, pardon me, my liege! But for my tears, the moist impediments to my speech, I would have forestalled this dear and deep rebuke before you with grief had spoken and I had heard the course of it so far. There is your crown; and He that wears the crown immortally long guard it yours! If I love it more than as your honor and as your renown, let me no more rise from this obedience, which my most inward true and dutiful spirit teaches in this prostrate and external bending. God witness with me, when I came in here, and found no breath within your Majesty, how cold it struck my heart! If I feign, oh, let me in my present wildness die and never live to show the incredulous world the noble change that I have purposed! Coming to look on you, thinking you dead, and dead almost, my liege, to think you were, I spoke unto this crown as having sense, and thus upbraided it: "The care depending on you has fed upon the body of my father; therefore you best of gold are worst of gold. Other, less fine in carat, is more precious, preserving life in drinkable medicine; but you, most fine, most honored, most renowned, have eaten your bearer up." Thus, my most royal liege, accusing it, I put it on my head, to try with it, as with an enemy that had before my face murdered my father, the quarrel of a true heir. But if it did infect my blood with joy, or swell my thoughts to any strain of pride, if any rebel or vain spirit of mine did with the least affection of a welcome give entertainment to the might of it, let God forever keep it from my head and make me as the poorest vassal is, that with awe and terror kneels to it!

HENRY IV. Oh my son, God put it in your mind to take it hence, that you might win the more your father's love, pleading so wisely in excuse of it! Come here, Harry, sit by my bed, and hear, I think, the very last counsel that ever I shall breathe. God knows, my son, by what byways and indirect crooked ways I met this crown, and I myself know well how troublesome it sat upon my head. To you it shall descend with better quiet, better opinion, better confirmation, for all the soil of the achievement goes with me into the earth. It seemed in me but as an honor snatched with boisterous hand, and I had many living to upbraid my gain of it by their assistance, which daily grew to quarrel and to bloodshed, wounding supposed peace. All these bold fears you see with peril I have answered; for all my reign has been but as a scene acting that argument. And now my death changes the manner, for what in me was acquired, falls upon you in a fairer way; so you wear the garland successively. Yet though you stand more sure than I could do, you are not firm enough, since griefs are green; and all my friends, which you must make your friends, have but their stings and teeth newly taken out; by whose fierce working I was first advanced and by whose power I well might lodge a fear of being again displaced; which to avoid, I cut them off, and had a purpose now to lead out many to the Holy Land, lest rest and lying still might make them look too close into my state. Therefore, my Harry, be it your course to busy giddy minds with foreign quarrels, that action, hence carried out, may waste the memory of the former days. More would I, but my lungs are wasted so that strength of speech is utterly denied me. How I came by the crown, oh God, forgive, and grant it may with you in true peace live!

PRINCE HENRY. My gracious liege, you won it, wore it, kept it, gave it me; then plain and right must my possession be, which I with more than with a common pain against all the world will rightfully maintain.
[Enter Lord John of Lancaster and others.]
HENRY IV. Look, look, here comes my John of Lancaster.
LANCASTER. Health, peace, and happiness to my royal father!

HENRY IV. You bring me happiness and peace, son John, but health, alas, with youthful wings has flown from this bare withered trunk. Upon your sight my worldly business makes a period. Where is my Lord of Warwick?
PRINCE HENRY. My Lord of Warwick!
[Enter Warwick and others.]
HENRY IV. Does any particular name belong to the lodging where I first swooned?
WARWICK. It is called Jerusalem, my noble lord.

HENRY IV. Praise be to God! Even there my life must end. It has been prophesied to me many years, that I should not die but in Jerusalem, which vainly I supposed the Holy Land. But bear me to that chamber; there I'll lie; in that Jerusalem shall Harry die.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — Gloucestershire. Shallow’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Shallow, Falstaff, Bardolph and Page.]
SHALLOW. By cock and pie, sir, you shall not leave tonight. What, Davy, I say!
FALSTAFF. You must excuse me, Master Robert Shallow.
SHALLOW. I will not excuse you, you shall not be excused. Excuses shall not be admitted, there is no excuse shall serve, you shall not be excused. Why, Davy!
[Enter Davy.]
DAVY. Here, sir.
SHALLOW. Davy, Davy, Davy, Davy, let me see, Davy, let me see, Davy, let me see. Yes, by Mary, William the cook, tell him to come here. Sir John, you shall not be excused.
DAVY. By Mary, sir, thus: those orders cannot be carried out; and again, sir — shall we sow the headland with wheat?
SHALLOW. With red wheat, Davy. But as for William cook, are there no young pigeons?
DAVY. Yes, sir. Here is now the smith's bill for shoeing and plough-irons.
SHALLOW. Let it be reckoned and paid. Sir John, you shall not be excused.
DAVY. Now, sir, a new link to the bucket must be had. And, sir, do you mean to dock any of William's wages, for the sack he lost the other day at Hinckley fair?
SHALLOW. He shall answer for it. Some pigeons, Davy, a couple of short-legged hens, a joint of mutton, and any pretty little tiny kickshaws, tell William cook.
DAVY. Does the man of war stay all night, sir?
SHALLOW. Yes, Davy, I will treat him well: a friend in the court is better than a penny in the purse. Treat his men well, Davy, for they are arrant knaves, and will backbite.
DAVY. No worse than they are backbitten, sir, for they have marvellously foul linen.
SHALLOW. Well thought of, Davy. About your business, Davy.
DAVY. I beg you, sir, to favor William Visor of Woncot against Clement Perkes of the hill.
SHALLOW. There are many complaints, Davy, against that Visor. That Visor is an arrant knave, to my knowledge.

DAVY. I grant your worship that he is a knave, sir, but yet, God forbid, sir, that a knave should not have some support at his friend's request. An honest man, sir, is able to speak for himself, when a knave is not. I have served your worship truly, sir, these eight years; and if I cannot once or twice in a quarter back a knave against an honest man, I have but very little credit with your worship. The knave is my honest friend, sir; therefore I beg your worship let him be supported.
SHALLOW. Get on; I say he shall have no wrong. Look about, Davy.
[Exit Davy.]
Where are you, Sir John? Come, come, come, off with your boots. Give me your hand, Master Bardolph.
BARDOLPH. I am glad to see your worship.
SHALLOW. I thank you with all my heart, kind Master Bardolph; and welcome, my tall fellow [to the Page]. Come, Sir John.
FALSTAFF. I'll follow you, good Master Robert Shallow.
[Exit Shallow.]
Bardolph, look to our horses.
[Exeunt Bardolph and Page.]

If I were sawed up into bits, I should make four dozen of such bearded hermits' staves as Master Shallow. It is a wonderful thing to see the similar coherence of his men's spirits and his own. They, by observing him, behave themselves like foolish justices: he, by conversing with them, is turned into a justice-like serving-man. Their spirits are so married in conjunction with the company they share that they flock together in consent, like so many wild geese. If I had a suit to make to Master Shallow, I would flatter his men with the implication of being close to their master: if to his men, I would butter up Master Shallow by saying no man could better command his servants. It is certain that either wise bearing or ignorant carriage is caught, as men catch diseases, from one another. Therefore let men take heed of their company. I will devise enough matter out of this Shallow to keep Prince Harry in continual laughter the wearing out of six fashions, which is four terms, or two lawsuits, and he shall laugh without intervals. Oh, it is much that a lie with a slight oath and a jest with a sad brow will do with a fellow who never had an ache in his shoulders! Oh, you shall see him laugh till his face is like a wet cloak ill laid up!
SHALLOW.
[Within.] Sir John!
FALSTAFF. I come, Master Shallow, I come, Master Shallow.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — Westminster. The palace
paragraphs: [Enter Warwick and the Lord Chief Justice, meeting.]
WARWICK. How now, my Lord Chief Justice, where away?
CHIEF JUSTICE. How is the King?
WARWICK. Exceedingly well. His cares are now all ended.
CHIEF JUSTICE. I hope, not dead.
WARWICK. He has walked the way of nature, and to our purposes he lives no more.
CHIEF JUSTICE. I wish his Majesty had called me with him. The service that I truly rendered his life has left me open to all injuries.
WARWICK. Indeed I think the young King does not love you.
CHIEF JUSTICE. I know he does not, and I arm myself to welcome the condition of the time, which cannot look more hideously upon me than I have drawn it in my imagination.
[Enter Lancaster, Clarence, Gloucester and others.]

WARWICK. Here comes the heavy offspring of dead Harry. Oh that the living Harry had the temper of him the worst of these three gentlemen! How many nobles then should hold their places, that must strike sail to spirits of vile sort!
CHIEF JUSTICE. Oh God, I fear all will be overturned.
LANCASTER. Good morrow, cousin Warwick, good morrow.
GLOUCESTER & CLARENCE. Good morrow, cousin.
LANCASTER. We meet like men who had forgotten to speak.
WARWICK. We do remember, but our subject is all too heavy to admit much talk.
LANCASTER. Well, peace be with him that has made us heavy!
CHIEF JUSTICE. Peace be with us, lest we be heavier!
GLOUCESTER. Oh, good my lord, you have lost a friend indeed; and I dare swear you do not borrow that face of seeming sorrow; it is surely your own.
LANCASTER. Though no man is assured what grace to find, you stand in coldest expectation. I am the sorrier; I wish it were otherwise.
CLARENCE. Well, you must now speak Sir John Falstaff fair, which swims against the stream of your quality.

CHIEF JUSTICE. Sweet Princes, what I did I did in honor, led by the impartial conduct of my soul; and you shall never see that I will beg a ragged and forestalled pardon. If truth and upright innocency fail me, I'll to the King my master that is dead, and tell him who has sent me after him.
WARWICK. Here comes the Prince.
[Enter King Henry the Fifth, attended.]
CHIEF JUSTICE. Good morrow, and God save your Majesty!

HENRY V. This new and gorgeous garment, majesty, sits not so easy on me as you think. Brothers, you mix your sadness with some fear. This is the English, not the Turkish court; not Amurath an Amurath succeeds, but Harry Harry. Yet be sad, good brothers, for, by my faith, it very well becomes you. Sorrow so royally in you appears that I will deeply put the fashion on and wear it in my heart. Why then, be sad; but entertain no more of it, good brothers, than a joint burden laid upon us all. For me, by heaven, I bid you be assured, I'll be your father and your brother too; let me but bear your love, I'll bear your cares. Yet weep that Harry's dead, and so will I; but Harry lives, who shall convert those tears by number into hours of happiness.
PRINCES. We hope no otherwise from your Majesty.
HENRY V. You all look strangely on me. And you most; you are, I think, assured I do not love you.
CHIEF JUSTICE. I am assured, if I be measured rightly, your Majesty has no just cause to hate me.

HENRY V. No? How might a prince of my great hopes forget such great indignities you laid upon me? What! Scold, rebuke, and roughly send to prison the immediate heir of England? Was this easy? May this be washed in Lethe and forgotten?

CHIEF JUSTICE. I then did embody the person of your father; the image of his power lay then in me; and in the administration of his law, while I was busy for the commonwealth, your Highness pleased to forget my place, the majesty and power of law and justice, the image of the King whom I represented, and struck me in my very seat of judgment; whereon, as an offender to your father, I gave bold way to my authority and did commit you. If the deed was ill, are you contented, wearing now the garland, to have a son set your decrees at nought? To pluck down justice from your awful bench? To trip the course of law and blunt the sword that guards the peace and safety of your person? No, more, to spurn at your most royal image, and mock your workings in a second body? Question your royal thoughts, make the case yours; be now the father and imagine yourself a son, hear your own dignity so much profaned, see your most dreadful laws so loosely slighted, behold yourself so by a son disdained, and then imagine me taking your part and in your power softly silencing your son. After this cold consideration, sentence me; and, as you are a king, speak in your state what I have done that misbecame my place, my person, or my liege's sovereignty.

HENRY V. You are right, justice, and you weigh this well. Therefore still bear the balance and the sword. And I do wish your honors may increase till you live to see a son of mine offend you and obey you, as I did. So shall I live to speak my father's words: "Happy am I, that I have a man so bold who dares do justice on my own son; and not less happy, having such a son who would deliver up his greatness so into the hands of justice." You did commit me, for which I do commit into your hand the unstained sword that you have used to bear, with this remembrance: that you use the same with the like bold, just, and impartial spirit as you have done against me. There is my hand. You shall be as a father to my youth, my voice shall sound as you do prompt my ear, and I will stoop and humble my intents to your well-practiced wise directions. And, princes all, believe me, I beseech you, my father is gone wild into his grave, for in his tomb lie my affections; and with his spirit sadly I survive to mock the expectation of the world, to frustrate prophecies, and to raze out rotten opinion, who has written me down after my seeming. The tide of blood in me has proudly flowed in vanity till now. Now does it turn and ebb back to the sea, where it shall mingle with the state of floods, and flow henceforth in formal majesty. Now call we our high court of parliament, and let us choose such limbs of noble counsel that the great body of our state may go in equal rank with the best-governed nation; that war, or peace, or both at once, may be as things known and familiar to us; in which you, father, shall have foremost hand. Our coronation done, we will summon, as I before remembered, all our state: and, God consigning to my good intents, no prince nor peer shall have just cause to say, God shorten Harry's happy life one day!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 3 — Gloucestershire. Shallow’s orchard
paragraphs: [Enter Falstaff, Shallow, Silence, Davy, Bardolph and the Page.]
SHALLOW. No, you shall see my orchard, where, in an arbor, we will eat a last year's pippin of my own grafting, with a dish of caraways, and so forth. Come, cousin Silence. And then to bed.
FALSTAFF. Before God, you have here a goodly dwelling, and a rich one.
SHALLOW. Barren, barren, barren; beggars all, beggars all, Sir John. By Mary, good air. Spread the table, Davy, spread, Davy. Well said, Davy.
FALSTAFF. This Davy serves you for good uses; he is your serving-man and your manager.
SHALLOW. A good rogue, a good rogue, a very good rogue, Sir John. By the mass, I have drunk too much sack at supper. A good rogue. Now sit down, now sit down. Come, cousin.
SILENCE. Ah, fellow! Quoth he, we shall [Singing.]
Do nothing but eat, and make good cheer, and praise God for the merry year, when flesh is cheap and women dear, and lusty lads roam here and there so merrily, and ever among so merrily.
FALSTAFF. There's a merry heart! Good Master Silence, I'll drink a health to you for that shortly.
SHALLOW. Give Master Bardolph some wine, Davy.

DAVY. Sweet sir, sit. I'll be with you shortly. Most sweet sir, sit. Master page, good master page, sit. Cheers! What you lack in food, we'll make up in drink, but you must bear with us; the heart is all.
[Exit.]
SHALLOW. Be merry, Master Bardolph, and, my little soldier there, be merry.
SILENCE.
[Singing.]
Be merry, be merry, my wife has all, for women are shrews, both short and tall. It's merry in the hall when beards wag all, and welcome merry Shrove-tide. Be merry, be merry.
FALSTAFF. I did not think Master Silence had been a man of this mettle.
SILENCE. Who, I? I have been merry twice and once before now.
[Enter Davy.]
DAVY.
[To Bardolph.] Here's a dish of russet apples for you.
SHALLOW. Davy!
DAVY. Your worship? I'll be with you straight away.
[To Bardolph.] A cup of wine, sir?
SILENCE.
[Singing.]
A cup of wine that's brisk and fine, and I'll drink to you, my sweetheart mine, and a merry heart lives long.
FALSTAFF. Well said, Master Silence.
SILENCE. If we shall be merry, now comes in the sweet of the night.
FALSTAFF. Health and long life to you, Master Silence.
SILENCE.
[Singing.]
Fill the cup, and let it come, I'll pledge you a mile to the bottom.

SHALLOW. Honest Bardolph, welcome! If you want anything and will not call, curse your heart. Welcome, my little tiny thief, [to the Page] and welcome indeed too. I'll drink to Master Bardolph, and to all the cavaliers about London.
DAVY. I hope to see London once before I die.
BARDOLPH. If I might see you there, Davy—
SHALLOW. By the mass, you'll crack a quart together, ha! Will you not, Master Bardolph?
BARDOLPH. Yes, sir, in a pottle-pot.
SHALLOW. By God's elves, I thank you. The knave will stick by you, I can assure you of that. He will not desert, he. He's true bred.
BARDOLPH. And I'll stick by him, sir.
SHALLOW. Why, there spoke a king. Lack nothing! Be merry.
[Knocking within.]
Look who's at the door there, ho! Who knocks?
[Exit Davy.]
FALSTAFF.
[To Silence, seeing him take off a bumper.] Why, now you have done me
right.
SILENCE.
[Singing.]
Do me right, and dub me knight: Samingo.
Isn't that so?
FALSTAFF. It is so.
SILENCE. Is it so? Why then, say an old man can do something.
[Enter Davy.]
DAVY. If it please your worship, there's one Pistol come from the court with news.
FALSTAFF. From the court? Let him come in.
[Enter Pistol.]
How now, Pistol?
PISTOL. Sir John, God save you!
FALSTAFF. What wind blew you here, Pistol?
PISTOL. Not the ill wind which blows no man to good. Sweet knight, you are now one of the greatest men in this realm.
SILENCE. By our lady, I think he is, except for goodman Puff of Barson.

PISTOL. Puff! Puff in your teeth, most recreant base coward! Sir John, I am your Pistol and your friend, and helter-skelter have I ridden to you, and tidings I bring and lucky joys, and golden times, and happy news of price.
FALSTAFF. Please now, deliver them like a man of this world.
PISTOL. A fig for the world and worldlings base! I speak of Africa and golden joys.
FALSTAFF. Oh base Assyrian knight, what is your news? Let King Cophetua know the truth of it.
SILENCE.
[Singing.] And Robin Hood, Scarlet, and John.
PISTOL. Shall dunghill curs confront the Helicons? And shall good news be baffled? Then, Pistol, lay your head in Furies' lap.
SHALLOW. Honest gentleman, I do not know your breeding.
PISTOL. Why then, lament for it.
SHALLOW. Give me pardon, sir. If, sir, you come with news from the court, I take it there are but two ways, either to utter them, or conceal them. I am, sir, under the King, in some authority.
PISTOL. Under which king, Besonian? Speak, or die.
SHALLOW. Under King Harry.
PISTOL. Harry the Fourth, or Fifth?
SHALLOW. Harry the Fourth.
PISTOL. A fig for your office! Sir John, your tender lambkin now is King; Harry the Fifth's the man. I speak the truth. When Pistol lies, do this, and fig me, like the bragging Spaniard.
FALSTAFF. What, is the old King dead?
PISTOL. As a nail in a door. The things I speak are just.
FALSTAFF. Away, Bardolph, saddle my horse. Master Robert Shallow, choose what office you will in the land, it's yours. Pistol, I will double-charge you with dignities.
BARDOLPH. Oh joyful day! I would not take a knighthood for my fortune.
PISTOL. What! I do bring good news.
FALSTAFF. Carry Master Silence to bed. Master Shallow, my Lord Shallow, be what you will; I am Fortune's steward! Get on your boots, we'll ride all night. Oh sweet Pistol! Away, Bardolph!
[Exit Bardolph.]

Come, Pistol, tell me more; and besides, devise something to do yourself good. Boots, boots, Master Shallow. I know the young King is sick to see me. Let us take any man's horses. The laws of England are at my command. Blessed are they that have been my friends, and woe to my Lord Chief Justice!
PISTOL. Let vultures vile seize on his lungs also! "Where is the life that late I led?" say they: why, here it is; welcome these pleasant days!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 4 — London. A street
paragraphs: [Enter Beadles, dragging in Hostess Quickly and Doll Tearsheet.]
HOSTESS. No, you arrant knave. I wish to God that I might die, that I might have you hanged. You have pulled my shoulder out of joint.
FIRST BEADLE. The constables have delivered her over to me, and she shall have whipping-cheer enough, I warrant her. There has been a man or two recently killed about her.

DOLL. Nut-hook, nut-hook, you lie! Come on, I'll tell you what, you damned tripe-faced rascal, if the child I now carry should miscarry, you would have been better off had you struck your own mother, you paper-faced villain.
HOSTESS. Oh the Lord, that Sir John were come! He would make this a bloody day for somebody. But I pray God the fruit of her womb miscarry!
FIRST BEADLE. If it does, you shall have a dozen of cushions again; you have only eleven now. Come, I order you both to go with me, for the man is dead that you and Pistol beat between you.

DOLL. I'll tell you what, you thin man in a censer, I will have you as soundly thrashed for this, you bluebottle rogue, you filthy famished prison-keeper, if you are not thrashed, I'll forswear half-kirtles.
FIRST BEADLE. Come, come, you she knight-errant, come.
HOSTESS. Oh God, that right should thus overcome might! Well, from suffering comes ease.
DOLL. Come, you rogue, come, bring me to a justice.
HOSTESS. Aye, come, you starved bloodhound.
DOLL. Goodman death, goodman bones!
HOSTESS. You skeleton, you!
DOLL. Come, you thin thing, come, you rascal!
FIRST BEADLE. Very well.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 5 — A public place near Westminster Abbey
paragraphs: [Enter two Grooms, strewing rushes.]
FIRST GROOM. More rushes, more rushes.
SECOND GROOM. The trumpets have sounded twice.
FIRST GROOM. It will be two o'clock before they come from the coronation. Hurry, hurry.
[Exeunt.]
[Trumpets sound, and the King and his train pass over the stage. Enter Falstaff, Shallow, Pistol, Bardolph and Page.]
FALSTAFF. Stand here by me, Master Robert Shallow. I will make the King show you favor. I will give him a knowing look as he comes by, and you just mark the countenance he will give me.
PISTOL. God bless your lungs, good knight!

FALSTAFF. Come here, Pistol, stand behind me. Oh, if I had had time to have made new liveries, I would have spent the thousand pounds I borrowed from you. But it doesn't matter, this poor show is better. This implies the zeal I had to see him.
SHALLOW. It does so.
FALSTAFF. It shows my earnestness of affection—
SHALLOW. It does so.
FALSTAFF. My devotion—
SHALLOW. It does, it does, it does.
FALSTAFF. As it were, to ride day and night, and not to deliberate, not to remember, not to have patience to change my clothes—
SHALLOW. It is best, certainly.

FALSTAFF. But to stand stained with travel, and sweating with desire to see him, thinking of nothing else, putting all other affairs in oblivion, as if there were nothing else to be done but to see him.
PISTOL. It is semper idem, for obsque hoc nihil est; it is all in every part.
SHALLOW. It is so, indeed.

PISTOL. My knight, I will inflame your noble liver, and make you rage. Your Doll, and Helen of your noble thoughts, is in base captivity and contagious prison, hauled there by most mechanical and dirty hand. Rouse up revenge from the ebon den with fell Alecto's snake, for Doll is in. Pistol speaks nothing but truth.
FALSTAFF. I will deliver her.
[Shouts within. The trumpets sound.]
PISTOL. There roared the sea, and trumpet-clangor sounds.
[Enter the King and his train, the Lord Chief Justice among them.]
FALSTAFF. God save your Grace, King Hal, my royal Hal!
PISTOL. The heavens guard and keep you, most royal child of fame!
FALSTAFF. God save you, my sweet boy!
HENRY V. My Lord Chief Justice, speak to that vain man.
CHIEF JUSTICE. Have you your wits? Do you know what it is you speak?
FALSTAFF. My King! My Jove! I speak to you, my heart!

HENRY V. I know thee not, old man. Fall to your prayers. How ill white hairs becomes a fool and jester! I have long dreamt of such a kind of man, so surfeit-swelled, so old, and so profane; but, being awakened, I do despise my dream. Make less your body hence, and more your grace; leave gormandizing; know the grave gapes for you three times wider than for other men. Don't reply to me with a fool-born jest. Don't presume that I am the thing I was; for God knows, and so shall the world perceive, that I have turned away my former self; so will I those that kept me company. When you hear I am as I have been, approach me, and you shall be as you were, the tutor and the feeder of my riots. Till then I banish you, on pain of death, as I have done the rest of my misleaders, not to come near our person by ten miles. For a competence of life I will allow you, that lack of means enforce you not to evils. And, as we hear you reform yourselves, we will, according to your strengths and qualities, give you advancement. Be it your charge, my lord, to see performed the tenor of our word. Set on.
[Exeunt King with his train.]
FALSTAFF. Master Shallow, I owe you a thousand pounds.
SHALLOW. Yes, by Mary, Sir John, which I beg you to let me have home with me.

FALSTAFF. That can hardly be, Master Shallow. Do not grieve at this; I shall be sent for in private to him. Look you, he must seem thus to the world. Fear not your advancements; I will be the man yet that shall make you great.
SHALLOW. I cannot perceive how, unless you give me your doublet and stuff me out with straw. I beg you, good Sir John, let me have five hundred of my thousand.
FALSTAFF. Sir, I will be as good as my word. This that you heard was but a pretense.
SHALLOW. A pretense that I fear you will die in, Sir John.
FALSTAFF. Fear no colors. Come with me to dinner. Come, Lieutenant Pistol; come, Bardolph. I shall be sent for soon at night.
[Enter the Lord Chief Justice and Prince John, Officers with them.]
CHIEF JUSTICE. Go, carry Sir John Falstaff to the Fleet. Take all his company along with him.
FALSTAFF. My lord, my lord—
CHIEF JUSTICE. I cannot speak now. I will hear you soon. Take them away.
PISTOL. Si fortuna me tormenta, spero me contenta.
[Exeunt all but Prince John and the Lord Chief Justice.]

LANCASTER. I like this fair proceeding of the King's. He intends his accustomed followers shall all be very well provided for, but all are banished till their behavior appears more wise and modest to the world.
CHIEF JUSTICE. And so they are.
LANCASTER. The King has called his parliament, my lord.
CHIEF JUSTICE. He has.

LANCASTER. I will lay odds that, before this year expires, we bear our civil swords and native fire as far as France. I heard a bird so sing, whose music, to my thinking, pleased the King. Come, will you hence?
[Exeunt.]
EPILOGUE.

First my fear; then my curtsy; last my speech. My fear is your displeasure; my curtsy, my duty; and my speech, to beg your pardons. If you look for a good speech now, you undo me, for what I have to say is of my own making; and what indeed I should say will, I fear, prove my own ruin. But to the purpose, and so to the venture. Let it be known to you, as it is very well, I was lately here at the end of a displeasing play, to ask your patience for it and to promise you a better. I meant indeed to pay you with this; which, if like an ill venture it comes unluckily home, I break, and you, my gentle creditors, lose. Here I promised you I would be, and here I commit my body to your mercies. Forgive me some, and I will pay you some, and, as most debtors do, promise you infinitely.

If my tongue cannot entreat you to acquit me, will you command me to use my legs? And yet that would be but light payment, to dance out of your debt. But a good conscience will make any possible satisfaction, and so would I. All the gentlewomen here have forgiven me; if the gentlemen will not, then the gentlemen do not agree with the gentlewomen, which was never seen before in such an assembly.

One word more, I beg you. If you are not too much cloyed with fat meat, our humble author will continue the story, with Sir John in it, and make you merry with fair Katharine of France; where, for all I know, Falstaff shall die of a sweat, unless already he be killed with your hard opinions; for Oldcastle died a martyr, and this is not the man. My tongue is weary; when my legs are too, I will bid you good night.
